I think sexigesimal (base 60) number systems were far more intuitive. 60 is the first number that 1 through 6 all divide equally (that's 12 factors in a very small number). 60-base number systems are still used for time, the calendar, GPS coordinates, trigonometry, and so much more! It also makes simple fractions SO much easier to deal with. In a base-10 system, you can't even express a VERY simple concept, such as 1/3. It can be expressed as a fraction, like I just did, but you can't write it accurately without the fraction. 0.3333333333..... It just keeps going. You can see how annoying it would be to an early merchant, when you can't accurately write a simple division problem without lots of "remainders" left over.

Even common terms you are used to using are actually artifacts of our old number system. Degrees, minutes and seconds are all 1/60 of the former. You probably even know the notations, without realizing it! You also may not have know that the symbol for "degree" is actually just a superscripted "0".

In medieval Latin texts, sexagesimal numbers were written using Hindu-Arabic numerals; the different levels of fractions were denoted minuta (i.e., fraction), minuta secunda, minuta tertia, etc. By the seventeenth century it became common to denote the integer part of sexagesimal numbers by a superscripted zero, and the various fractional parts by one or more accent marks.
